datasets.effective_resolution: See local effective-resolution raster; not assumed equal to nominal
datasets.horizontal_reference_system: Moon (2015) Sphere / Ocentric / South Polar; MOON_DE421 reference frame
datasets.vertical_reference_system: Elevation units in metres; reference datum defined by LOLA project
datasets.processing_level: Level-1 (raw range data processed into DEM; adjusted/blended construction)

datasets.name: Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation CTX DTM Mosaic
datasets.producing_institution: USGS Astrogeology Science Center / NASA MRO CTX
datasets.spatial_coverage: Jezero crater and Mars 2020 landing region; 18.211 to 18.7212 N, 77.1605 to 77.699 E
datasets.horizontal_reference_system: Equirectangular planetary CRS; MOLA control preserved
datasets.vertical_reference_system: Elevation units in metres; referenced to delta geoid
datasets.processing_level: Level-1 (derived CTM/DTM mosaic from MRO CTX imagery)
datasets.notes: Jezero-specific; created for terrain-relative navigation. Equirectangular CRS and MOLA control must be preserved. Not suitable as a fully independent global reference but valid for localized benchmarking.

datasets.name: NASADEM Merged DEM Global 1 arc second V001
datasets.spatial_coverage: Global; 1 arc-second (~30 m nominal) global coverage
datasets.nominal_resolution: 1 arc-second, approximately 30 m; latitude-dependent ground spacing

datasets.name: Synthetic flat DEM benchmark
datasets.notes: Synthetic test-only dataset; does not represent real terrain. Used for software regression, not scientific inference.

datasets.name: Synthetic gradient DEM benchmark
datasets.notes: Synthetic test-only dataset; does not represent real terrain. Used for software regression, not scientific inference.

limitation: No independently labeled real benchmark dataset was available covering overlapping terrain across two+ DEM products. Existing datasets (moon_lola, mars_jezero_ctx_dtm) are validated observational products but cover different geographical regions. earth_nasadem_hgt_v001 is blocked by authentication. No dataset pair currently enables within-pair TMSI reproducibility testing.

list.name: Atacama Desert
list.scientific_description: The Atacama Desert is the driest non-polar desert on Earth, with some areas experiencing no rainfall for centuries. Its hyper-arid conditions and extreme elevation variations make it a compelling analog for Mars' arid landscapes and ancient paleoenvironments.
list.selection_rationale: Mars mission planners use Atacama as a test site for instrument validation and habitability studies. Its soil chemistry and arid geomorphology closely resemble hypothesized Martian paleoenvironments.
list.supporting_references: NASA Mars Analog Research Program; USGS Astrogeology Science Center publications
list.known_limitations: No direct in-situ Mars comparison; elevation data from secondary sources only; aridity extremes vary spatially
list.geological_context: Hyper-arid erg dunes and playas over Precambrian basement; minimal vegetation; alluvial fan deposits with ancient paleochannels.

list.name: Antarctica Polar Plateau
list.scientific_description: The Antarctic Polar Plateau is the highest, driest, and coldest region on Earth. Its ice-covered terrain and frozen sediment layers make it an analog for Mars' polar caps and Moon's permanently shadowed regions.
list.selection_rationale: Ice sheet dynamics, frozen ground physics, and sublimation processes in Antarctica are studied as analogs for Martian polar cap evolution and lunar polar volatiles. Orbital radar data (SHARAD, MARSIS) comparison possible.
list.supporting_references: NSF US Antarctic Program; IPCC cryosphere assessments; peer-reviewed glaciology publications
list.known_limitations: Ice dynamics differ from rigid lunar/Martian regolith; seasonal variability not applicable to airless bodies
list.geological_context: Ice-covered plateau with frozen sediment layers, sublimation features, and exposed blue-ice areas; sedimentary basins overridden by ice sheet.

list.name: Hawaii Island Volcanic Landscapes
list.scientific_description: Hawaii Island features active and dormant basaltic volcanoes with diverse lava flow morphologies, from pahoehoe to 'a'ā. Its volcanic terrain is a direct analog for Mars' shield volcanoes and Moon's mare basalt units.
list.selection_rationale: Hawaii's volcanic rock types, flow textures, and volcanic landforms (calderas, rift zones, lava tubes) are studied as analogs for Martian shield volcanoes (e.g., Olympus Mons) and lunar mare basalt units. Subsurface lava tube studies inform robotic exploration planning.
list.supporting_references: USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory; peer-reviewed volcanology publications; NASA SSERV program
list.known_limitations: Tropical climate processes not applicable to arid/airless bodies; active volcanic systems differ from dormant/extinct Martian volcanoes
list.geological_context: Active basaltic shield volcanoes with pahoehoe and 'a' flow fields, calderas, rift zones, and young lava tubes; volcaniclastics and pyroclastic deposits.

list.name: Grand Canyon
list.scientific_description: The Grand Canyon exposes nearly 2 billion years of Earth's geological history in its layered sedimentary rocks. Its incision-driven topography makes it an analog for Valles Marineris and other martian canyon systems.
list.selection_rationale: Valles Marineris shares similarities with terrestrial canyons carved by water and wind erosion. The Grand Canyon's layered stratigraphy, slope profiles, and erosional features are studied to understand martian canyon formation processes and wind/ water action comparisons.
list.supporting_references: National Park Service geology reports; USGS Colorado Plateau studies; peer-reviewed geomorphology publications
list.source_dataset: USGS 3DEP; NASA Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) comparative studies
list.known_limitations: Fluvial processes on Earth differ from wind-dominated martian processes; gravity (3.71 m/s² vs 9.81 m/s²) changes erosion dynamics fundamentally
list.geological_context: Nearly 2 billion years of stratified sedimentary rock layers exposed by Colorado River incision; paleoenvironments from marine to fluvial.

list.name: Arabian Desert
list.scientific_description: The Arabian Desert encompasses hyper-arid sand seas (ergs), gravel plains (reg), and ancient river channels (wadis). Its desert morphology and sedimentary basins make it an analog for Mars' ergs and ancient fluvial environments.
list.selection_rationale: Mars orbiters (MRO, ODYSSEUS) have identified ergs and wadi systems that mimic Arabian Desert morphology. Sand dune dynamics, wadi incision, and evaporite deposits are comparable. Desert varnish and wind ripple patterns provide analog frameworks.
list.supporting_references: USGS desert geology studies; peer-reviewed aeolian sedimentology publications; NASA Mars analog field campaigns
list.source_dataset: USGS 3DEP; SRTM; orbiter DEM comparison datasets
list.known_limitations: No direct in-situ Mars comparison; sedimentary processes differ in reduced gravity; climate regimes are distinct
list.geological_context: Sand seas (ergs), gravel plains (regs), and ancient wadi channels with alluvial fans; aeolian sedimentary structures and evaporite deposits.

list.name: Death Valley
list.scientific_description: Death Valley is the hottest, driest low-elevation desert in North America. Its basin-and-range topography, extreme temperatures, and seasonal flash floods make it an analog for Mars' low-elevation basins and ancient fluvial periods.
list.selection_rationale: Basin topography, playa deposits, and alluvial fan systems in Death Valley are studied as analogs for martian basins and ancient lake beds. Elevation extremes and temperature ranges inform habitability and surface process studies.
list.supporting_references: National Park Service geology; USGS Death Valley field studies; peer-reviewed basin-and-range geomorphology publications
list.source_dataset: USGS 3DEP; SRTM; NASA orbital DEM comparisons
list.known_limitations: Terrestrial climate and gravity differ from Mars; no direct in-situ comparison possible; evaporation rates differ fundamentally
list.geological_context: Basin-and-range topography with evaporite deposits, alluvial fan systems, and playa (dry lake) deposits; extreme temperature regime.

list.name: Mojave Desert
list.scientific_description: The Mojave Desert encompasses transition zone geography between the Great Basin and Colorado Desert, featuring playas, alluvial fans, and bajadas. Its extreme aridity and basin topography make it a compelling analog for Mars' ancient arid environments and desiccated lake beds.
list.selection_rationale: Mars orbiters have identified playas and desiccated lake basins that mimic Mojave morphology. Soil chemistry and aeolian processes are comparable. The Mojave Mars Analog Field Station (MMAFS) is used for instrument validation.
list.supporting_references: NASA Mars Analog Research Program; USGS desert geology studies; peer-reviewed aeolian sedimentology publications; MMAFS documentation
list.source_dataset: USGS 3DEP; SRTM; NASA orbital DEM comparisons
list.known_limitations: No direct in-situ Mars comparison; elevation data from secondary sources only; climate regime distinct from ancient Mars
list.geological_context: Transition zone between Great Basin and Colorado Desert; playas, alluvial fans, bajadas over volcanic and sedimentary basement; dry lake basins.

list.name: Sahara Desert
list.country: Multiple (Chad, Egypt, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Morocco, Niger, Sudan, Tunisia)
list.scientific_description: The Sahara Desert is the world's largest hot desert, featuring expansive sand seas (ergs), gravel plains (regs), and ancient river channels (wadis). Its hyper-arid conditions and extensive dune fields make it a key analog for Mars' ergs and paleofluvial environments.
list.selection_rationale: Mars orbiters (MRO, ODYSSEUS) have identified ergs and wadi systems that mimic Sahara morphology. Sand dune dynamics, wadi incision, and evaporite deposits are comparable. Desert varnish and wind ripple patterns provide analog frameworks.
list.supporting_references: USGS desert geology studies; peer-reviewed aeolian sedimentology publications; NASA Mars analog field campaigns; orbital DEM comparison datasets
list.source_dataset: USGS 3DEP; SRTM; orbiter DEM comparison datasets
list.known_limitations: No direct in-situ Mars comparison; sedimentary processes differ in reduced gravity; climate regimes are distinct
list.geological_context: Extensive sand seas (ergs), gravel plains (regs), and ancient wadi/channels; fossil river valleys and aeolian sedimentary structures.

list.name: Arctic Tundra
list.scientific_description: The Arctic Tundra features permafrost, seasonal thaw lakes, and low-centered ice polygons. Its frozen ground physics and sublimation processes make it an analog for Mars' polar caps and Moon's permanently shadowed regions where volatiles freeze and cycle.
list.selection_rationale: Ice sheet dynamics, frozen ground physics, and sublimation processes in the Arctic are studied as analogs for Martian polar cap evolution and lunar polar volatiles. Orbital radar data (SHARAD, MARSIS) comparison possible. Permafrost degradation patterns inform predictions of polar volatile behavior.
list.supporting_references: NSF US Arctic Program; IPCC cryosphere assessments; peer-reviewed glaciology publications; SHARAD/MARSIS radar comparison studies
list.known_limitations: Ice dynamics differ from rigid lunar/Martian regolith; seasonal variability not applicable to airless bodies; reduced gravity effects on permafrost not fully characterized
list.geological_context: Permafrost terrain with seasonal thaw lakes, low-centered ice polygons, patterned ground, and frozen sediment layers; cryoturbation features.

list.name: Alaska Peninsula Volcanics
list.scientific_description: The Alaska Peninsula features active and dormant basaltic volcanoes with diverse lava flow morphologies, from pahoehoe to 'a'ā. Its volcanic terrain is a direct analog for Mars' shield volcanoes and Moon's mare basalt units at higher latitudes than Hawaii.
list.selection_rationale: Hawaii's volcanic rock types, flow textures, and landforms (calderas, rift zones) are studied as analogs for Martian shield volcanoes and lunar mare basalts. Alaska's higher latitude adds climate variability not present in Hawaii, informing studies of volcanic degradation across planetary latitudes.
list.supporting_references: USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory; Alaska Volcano Observatory; peer-reviewed volcanology publications; NASA SSERV program
list.known_limitations: Tropical climate processes not applicable to arid/airless bodies; active volcanic systems differ from dormant/extinct Martian volcanoes; higher precipitation regime
list.geological_context: Basaltic shield volcanoes and lava flow fields with calderas, rift zones, and young lava tubes; volcaniclastics and flow breccias.

list.name: Columbia River Flood Basalts
list.scientific_description: The Columbia River Flood Basalts comprise one of the world's largest continental flood basalt provinces, with thick layered lava flows covering thousands of kilometers. Its extensive basaltic terrain makes it an analog for Mars' extensive flood basalt provinces and lunar mare flooding events.
list.selection_rationale: Mars' Tharsis province and other flood basalt units are extensively studied via orbital data. The Columbia River Basalts' flow morphology, vesicle patterns, and weathering profiles provide ground-truth for orbital identification of similar units on Mars. Vast areal coverage enables statistical analysis of flow units.
list.supporting_references: USGS Geological surveys; peer-reviewed volcanology publications; NASA Mars orbiter comparative studies; geological mapping projects
list.source_dataset: USGS 3DEP; SRTM; NASA Mars orbiter DEM comparisons
list.known_limitations: Reduced gravity (3.71 m/s² vs 9.81 m/s²) changes flow dynamics fundamentally; tropical climate processes not applicable to airless bodies; weathering profiles differ without liquid water
list.geological_context: Extensive continental flood basalt province with thick layered lava flows, vesiclezoning, and flow-scale weathering profiles; geological sections documented.

list.name: Meteor Crater
list.scientific_description: Meteor Crater (Barringer Crater) in Arizona is a well-preserved simple impact structure approximately 1.2 km diameter. Its form and ejecta blanket make it the quintessential analog for martian impact craters, particularly simple craters in the 1-2 km range.
list.selection_rationale: Meteor Crater's morphometry, ejecta distribution, and rock fragment distribution have been extensively studied and directly compared to martian crater populations. Impact crater scaling laws derived from terrestrial data are essential for estimating impactor sizes and frequencies on Mars from crater counts.
list.supporting_references: USGS impact cratering studies; peer-reviewed planetary geology publications; NASA SSERV program; Meteor Crater Enterprises
list.known_limitations: Terrestrial gravity (9.81 m/s²) vs Mars (3.71 m/s²) changes ejecta dynamics; atmospheric effects differ (Earth has breathable air, Mars does not); crater modification processes differ between bodies
list.geological_context: Simple impact crater (1.2 km diameter) with well-preserved ejecta blanket, rim morphology, and fractured target rocks; impactites and shock-metamorphic features.

list.name: Lake Baikal Region
list.scientific_description: Lake Baikal and its surrounding region feature ancient rift valley topography, fluvial terraces, and glacial geomorphology. Its deeply incised valleys and ancient lake sediments make it an analog for martian rift valley systems and ancient lake basins.
list.selection_rationale: Mars orbiters have identified ancient rift valleys and lakebed deposits that mimic Baikal's geomorphology. Deltaic features, shoreline terraces, and fluvial incision patterns in the Baikal region provide comparative ground truth for orbited observations of martian paleolake systems.
list.supporting_references: Russian Academy of Sciences publications; peer-reviewed geomorphology studies; NASA Mars orbiter comparative investigations; rift valley mapping projects
list.known_limitations: Rift formation processes differ from impact/volcanic martian basins; lake sedimentation rates and chemistry differ in reduced gravity; continental location vs martian hemisphere distribution
list.geological_context: Rift valley topography with ancient lake sediments, fluvial terraces, glacial landforms, and deltaic deposits at river mouths.
